ACADEMIC INTEGRITY: YOUR WORK, YOUR SUCCESS

At SFU, you are expected to act honestly and responsibly in all your academic work. Cheating, plagiarism, or any other form of academic dishonesty harms your own learning, undermines the efforts of your classmates who pursue their studies honestly, and goes against the core values of the university.

To learn more about the academic disciplinary process and relevant academic supports, visit: 

  • SFU’s Academic Integrity Policy: S10-01 Policy
  • SFU’s Academic Integrity website, which includes helpful videos and tips in plain language: Academic Integrity at SFU

info.requirements:
Course requirements are pretty self-explanatory, except for the rabbit holes.  Most of these poets—Hayes and Coleman in particular—use a lot of allusions.  A “rabbit hole” is simply you asking, “What do I need to know in order to understand this poem?” and then tracking it down on the Internet and/or in the library resources online—and, as necessary, tracking down what you need to know in order to understand what you need to know.  You get 1 point for tracking down something useful about the poet or poem, ideally something the prof didn’t know (easier than you might think), 2 points for showing how it illuminates the poet or poem, and 3 points for a hermeneutic tour de force.  You must travel down at least one rabbit hole per week, and may do as many as five.  For example, if you read Coleman’s “Black Alice Laments (—after Lewis Carroll)”, and you note that the title refers to Alice in Wonderland, no points, because duh.  Track down the poem’s repeated references to Xanadu as references to Coleridge’s “Kubla Khan,” one grudging point (barely).  Persuasively identify a link between Coleridge and Carroll, two points.  Use that link to nail the meaning of the poem, three points.  (If this seems hard, it isn't: students KILL this part of the course.)
Another note: in this class, "draft" does not mean "6 sketchy pages, then a few words about what the rest will probably look like."  It means the absolute best you can do, so in revision we can take your work to the next level, which is what that "W" designation is all about.  Drafts that fail to meet this standard will not be accepted.
